title: 2 Samuel 5:17–25
context: 2 Samuel 5:17–25 records two Philistine attacks in the valley of Rephaim after David becomes king of all Israel. Each time David inquires of the LORD. The first time he is told to go up, and he wins at Baal Perazim, which the WEB footnote explains means "Lord who breaks out"; the Philistines abandon their idols. The second time he is told to circle around and wait for the sound of marching in the tops of the mulberry trees, a sign that the LORD has gone out before him. Both traditions highlight David’s dependence on the LORD’s guidance and the LORD fighting for his people.

verses.text: When the Philistines heard that they had anointed David king over Israel, all the Philistines went up to seek David, but David heard about it and went down to the stronghold.
verses.arminianNotes: When the Philistines hear that David has been anointed king over Israel, they come looking for him, and David goes down to the stronghold. Arminians see the new king’s unity of the nation drawing immediate opposition, which tests whether he will rely on the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that the stronghold here may be the same as earlier strongholds in David’s life, and interpreters debate its location. Both traditions read the verse as the beginning of a test that David meets by seeking God’s guidance.

verses.text: Now the Philistines had come and spread themselves in the valley of Rephaim.
verses.arminianNotes: The Philistines spread out in the valley of Rephaim. Arminians see a real military threat near Jerusalem, which sets up David’s response of inquiring of the LORD rather than acting on his own judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the valley of Rephaim lies southwest of Jerusalem. Both traditions read the verse as the setting for a battle in which the LORD will show that he fights for his people.

verses.text: David inquired of the LORD, saying, “Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you deliver them into my hand?” The LORD said to David, “Go up; for I will certainly deliver the Philistines into your hand.”
verses.arminianNotes: David asks the LORD whether to go up and whether he will deliver the Philistines into his hand, and the LORD says, "Go up." Arminians see David’s dependence on God as a model, with God answering a sincere request for guidance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that the promise of victory comes from God before the battle. Both traditions note that David’s practice of inquiring of the LORD contrasts with Saul’s failures (1 Samuel 28:6), and both see it as a mark of a godly king.

verses.text: David came to Baal Perazim, and David struck them there. Then he said, “The LORD has broken my enemies before me, like the breach of waters.” Therefore he called the name of that place Baal Perazim.
verses.arminianNotes: David defeats the Philistines at Baal Perazim and says the LORD broke his enemies like a breach of waters. The WEB footnote explains that the name means "Lord who breaks out." Arminians see David giving God the credit and naming the place as a memorial.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see the image of bursting waters as the LORD’s overwhelming power. Both traditions note that the same idea of the LORD breaking out appears in 6:8 with Uzzah, which links God’s power for his people and his holiness among them.

verses.text: They left their images there, and David and his men took them away.
verses.arminianNotes: The Philistines leave their images there, and David and his men carry them off. Arminian readers see the helplessness of idols that cannot even save themselves, a reversal of 1 Samuel 4–5, when the Philistines captured the ark.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. The parallel in 1 Chronicles 14:12 says David ordered the images burned, in line with the law (Deuteronomy 7:5, 25). Both traditions read the verse as showing the LORD’s victory over the gods of the nations.

verses.text: The Philistines came up yet again and spread themselves in the valley of Rephaim.
verses.arminianNotes: The Philistines come up again and spread out in the valley of Rephaim. Arminians see that one victory does not end every threat, so David must again seek God rather than assume the same approach will work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the repeated attack sets up the different instructions in the next verse. Both traditions read the verse as teaching continued dependence on God rather than relying on past success.

verses.text: When David inquired of the LORD, he said, “You shall not go up. Circle around behind them, and attack them in front of the mulberry trees.
verses.arminianNotes: When David inquires again, the LORD says not to go up but to circle behind them and attack in front of the mulberry trees. Arminians see David’s humility in asking again, and they see God giving new guidance for a new situation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that God directs the strategy, not only the outcome. Both traditions read the verse as a lesson that obedience means following God’s specific guidance rather than repeating a method that worked before.

verses.text: When you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the mulberry trees, then stir yourself up; for then the LORD has gone out before you to strike the army of the Philistines.”
verses.arminianNotes: When David hears the sound of marching in the tops of the mulberry trees, he is to act, for the LORD has gone out before him. Arminians see the sign as God’s assurance of his presence, calling David to act when God signals.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see the image of the LORD marching ahead as God fighting for his people, a theme of holy war. The identity of the trees is uncertain. Both traditions see the verse as stressing that the victory belongs to the LORD.

verses.text: David did so, as the LORD commanded him, and struck the Philistines all the way from Geba to Gezer.
verses.arminianNotes: David does as the LORD commanded and strikes the Philistines from Geba to Gezer. Arminian readers see obedience leading to victory and see the verse as the summary of a king who listens to God, in contrast with Saul.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that the parallel in 1 Chronicles 14:16 reads Gibeon for Geba. Both traditions read "as the LORD commanded him" as the key phrase, showing God’s blessing on a king who obeys his word.
